body_text:
### Proposal

Related to #4192 & #4122.

Hey, my goal is to implement the Remote Read protocol on top of my own storage and I'm trying to reduce the number of outgoing samples to shrink a response size. Basically, I'd like to push down the downsampling operation to my storage, and apply the logic of vanilla `query_range` to filter out samples that will be excluded by caller itself. 

But, both `start_timestamp_ms` in `Query` and `start_ms` in `ReadHint` contain the same value. And this value is affected by `lookbackDelta` configured on caller side, so if the original query is in the range `[t0, t1]`, remote read query will be in the range `[t0-lookbackDelta, t1]`. 

Unfortunately, since `lookbackDelta` is a configurable parameter, I have no idea how to calculate the original `t0` here. And without original `t0` it's impossible to reproduce a grid of the original `query_range` and align samples in the same way.  

So, the proposal is to pass `lookbackDelta` explicitly on each Remote Read request.
title: Add LookbackDelta to ReadHints

### Proposal

Hey

So, we have the usecase that we have one central prometheus instance and developers do not have access to the prometheus configuration. We are scraping consul for our metrics targets. While applications can provide their own labels, there is also certain data that the application doesn't know of, for example its (dynamic) id in our deployment system. What we'd like to be able to do, is to have some generic consul tag where can extract promtheus labels from.

For example with this config:

```
      - source_labels: [__meta_consul_tags]
        regex: "(?:^|.*?,)prom_label__(.+?)=(.+?)(?:$|,.*?)"
        action: replace
        target_label: $1
        replacement: $2
```

Given these consul tags:

```
a=b,b=c,prom_label__f=g,t=e,prom_label__z=l,l=o
```

I'd expect these labels in prometheus for the given target:

```
f=g,z=l
```

The workaround would be to manually list the labels for all services, which could be quite a lot.

I've already looked at the code and guess that we can easily change the regex code to use multiple matches instead of just one set of submatches. Adjusting the tests is an easy feat as well. This should imo not be a breaking change.
title: Turn one source label into multiple target labels

body_text:
### Proposal

This is an issue to kick start a discussion to switch the default configuration for the out-of-order window. 

Today the default value of the window is `0` **meaning no out-of-order samples are allowed into Prometheus by default**. it's up to the client to allow this use case and thus its up to the client to toggle the window and set it to a certain amount of minutes.

If we use Prometheus in the traditional way were it is pull based and it does scrapes based on a the configured interval this is completely fine and probably the out-of-order feature won't be needed.

However if Prometheus is used with remote-write due to a specific use case, certain network topologies, OTEL ingestion, scale or other reasons then we might run into issues. It's a paradigm change where order is hard to maintain. 

It is this second use case where enabling out-of-order by default to a small window like `5m` or `10m` starts making a bit of sense.
- An example is using Prometheus with OTEL. Due to how OTEL clients work, encouraging users to batch up writes and then remote writing them all at once to improve compression rate, out-of-order is a natural outcome.

For any of these cases, the user needs to know about the existence of this feature and how to tweak it to avoid data loss. Maybe it does make sense to enable it to a small window to solve 99% of the race conditions between the writes?

body_text:
### Problem

Relates to https://docs.google.com/document/d/1epvoO_R7JhmHYsII-GJ6Yw99Ky91dKOqOtZGqX7Bk0g/edit#heading=h.4lju4hrri2ch `Resource Attributes and their mapping` section.

This issue is intended as an umbrella issue to address the various problems that come from supporting natively OTEL resource attributes. There are two cases that we want to support:
- Application pushing metrics through the OTEL Collector.
- Application instrumented with OTEL SDK exposing metrics through /metrics and Prometheus scraping them.

We want both cases to be handled equally so that the ingestion method is not part of the problem.

### Proposal

The OTEL spec says that everything that is a resource attribute goes into `target_info`. One potential solution today is that Prometheus copy these attributes into series labels.

One way to do this is by setting up a config that specifies which attributes need to be mapped as labels. This config can be used for the both usecases that we have to support.
title: Handle OTEL resource attributes

### Proposal

We just had an incident where one of our Prometheus instances was not appending any samples to storage. We manage a fleet of Prometheus with very different sizes. We could create an alert with `prometheus_tsdb_head_active_appenders == 0` but it could become noisy.

With `prometheus_{tsdb_head|scrape}_appends_total` and `prometheus_{tsdb_head|scrape}_append_errors_total`, we could create an SLO for this case and be more proactive to such failures in the future.

body_text:
### Proposal

Being able to quickly see the running configuration on a Prometheus instance using the `/config` UI endpoint is a really convenient feature of Prometheus. However, with the recent addition of being able to separate scrape configs into multiple files with `scrape_config_files`, you lose the ability to see exactly what the full running config actually is when using it. This can make it more difficult to easily see what relabeling is happening on individual scrape jobs. 

Instead, you just see which paths are being included in the main config file, like so:
![Screenshot 2023-07-21 at 11 20 34 AM](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/assets/11506822/4314228b-2716-48f9-bedc-c93df0f65c5f)

I'd propose that the contents in the `/config` endpoint be expanded to show the contents of the included `scrape_config_files`.

In order to do so, I'm not sure if the best way would be to just include it in the box that is there now or create a new section named something like "Running Configuration" that has all of the scrape config files expanded. Or to create a new endpoint entirely just for scrape configs, similar to `/rules`.

Regardless, I believe it's an important feature and wanted to put this out there for ideas and tracking.
title: Expand scrape_config_files in the /config web UI endpoint

body_text:
### Proposal

Use case: make Prometheus scrape only local pods in Kubernetes i.e. pods running on the same host as the Prometheus pod. It's not easy to do that without hacks at the moment. Sysdig has this hack:

https://docs.sysdig.com/en/docs/sysdig-monitor/integrations/integration-library/prometheus-integrations/knative/

```
  relabel_configs:
  - action: keep
    source_labels: [__meta_kubernetes_pod_host_ip]
    regex: __HOSTIPS__
```

Some middle layer replaces `__HOSTIPS__` with the host IP. Another user wandering about the same use-case: https://www.reddit.com/r/kubernetes/comments/yre79j/prometheus_scrape_pods_only_on_the_current_node/

This could be exposed to k8s pods through:

```
  env:
    - name: NODE_IP
      valueFrom:
        fieldRef:
          fieldPath: status.hostIP
```

Now it is just needed to be able to use environment variables in relabel_configs. The only problem that I can think of is how to handle `${}` inside the regular expression because these characters mean something different inside `[]` in a regex.

Thanos has a reloader functionality in the Sidecar that replaces `$()` with environment variable's value everywhere in the file but it would be cool to have this natively in Prometheus.
title: Expand environment variables in relabel_configs

body_text:
### What did you do?

We have Prometheus(2.44.0) using remote write to Mimir(2.8.0) and the Mimir remote write endpoint becomes unavailable for 30m

### What did you expect to see?

Prometheus to fill up shard queue, retry writes during the outage and once endpoint becomes ready to upload the data

### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

Prometheus re-shards during the outage causing forced data flush of current shards that cannot happen and after `1m` of default flush timeout drops data

I suspect that there might be a bug in the threshold that should stop Prometheus from resharding if the endpoint is down (there are no successful writes)
https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/096ceca44f79a6f6ba9e31f7e5695d84d1cca330/storage/remote/queue_manager.go#L1474

I believe this timestamp should be set only if sending finished without error. 
The comment about using the values for re-sharding does not actually use this value, it uses timestamp from highestSentTimestamp metric
https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/096ceca44f79a6f6ba9e31f7e5695d84d1cca330/storage/remote/queue_manager.go#L982C31-L982C51

This would cause that even failed sends would update the last send timestamp and Prometheus would reshard even during outage causing data loss.

We have Prometheus(2.44.0) using remote write to Mimir(2.8.0) and the Mimir remote write endpoint becomes unavailable for 30m

### What did you expect to see?

Prometheus to fill up shard queue, retry writes during the outage and once endpoint becomes ready to upload the data

### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

Prometheus re-shards during the outage causing forced data flush of current shards that cannot happen and after `1m` of default flush timeout drops data

I suspect that there might be a bug in the threshold that should stop Prometheus from resharding if the endpoint is down (there are no successful writes)
https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/096ceca44f79a6f6ba9e31f7e5695d84d1cca330/storage/remote/queue_manager.go#L1474

I believe this timestamp should be set only if sending finished without error. 
The comment about using the values for re-sharding does not actually use this value, it uses timestamp from highestSentTimestamp metric
https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/096ceca44f79a6f6ba9e31f7e5695d84d1cca330/storage/remote/queue_manager.go#L982C31-L982C51

This would cause that even failed sends would update the last send timestamp and Prometheus would reshard even during outage causing data loss.

# Additional Endpoints Proposal This proposal is tangential to https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/12120, the initial "payload too large" problem prompted me to explore the possibility of adding additional endpoints. ## Preface I'm an engineer on the Grafana Alerting team, my primary focus is on the UI and front-end experience. The following proposal is not focused solely on Grafana as a consumer of the Prometheus API, I do believe however that having worked with Prometheus and Grafana for a good while now that this gives a unique perspective on a key area we want to improve – making Prometheus and its ecosystem the best choice for very large alerting setups. ## What is proposed As an alternative – but not mutually exclusive to – pagination we want to explore adding additional API endpoints to reduce the payload size of responses sent to an API consumer (like the Prometheus UI). These additional endpoint would allow progressively loading more data as the user navigates through the rule hierarchy. ## Why we're proposing it We've observed several users of Prometheus who are bringing a very large amount of alert rules with them to be visualized in a UI. We've also observed API responses in excess of several megabytes of data, with several contributing factors; the amount of alert rules and the amount of alerts for each invidual rule in particular. In order for the user not to have to wait several seconds for the UI to show anything at all there are several ways to incrementally show info about their alerts. This proposal explores adding additional API endpoints so we can render data sooner and consequently load only the data for groups or rules they are interested in. ## Prerequisites Some concepts are currently missing in Prometheus to allow additional endpoints to focus on a singular resource type; mainly identifiers. Using identifiers for each resource type will also simplify pagination with cursors later (see future work). Before implementing additional RESTful endpoints we should consider the following; 1. Returning unique group identifiers 1. Adding unique identifiers to alert rules 1. Consider introducing "namespaces" as an API resource ### Unique group identifier The `file name + group name` combination is unique in Prometheus. In order to fetch information about a single group we'd need a way for a group to be uniquely identifiable. We can't use the group name in that case since the name of the group is not unique across multiple file names. We can return the [group identifier](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/8f1dc4a70fe664e54482782aead7931b8a49a380/rules/manager.go#L474-L480) as part of the JSON response. ### Unique identifiers for alert rules It's currently allowed to add multiple identical alert rules to a group. In other words, the combination of `file name + group name + rule name` is not unique. We should ignore identical alert rules in a group (identified by its attributes) and using a hash to uniquely identify an alert rule across groups and files - `hash(file, group, rule attributes)` would guarantee unique alert rule identifiers for the entire Prometheus instance. ### Introducing "namespaces" Taking it one step further we could explore adding the concept of namespaces – this allows segmenting groups and alert rules on an additional level in the UI. Some DBs like Cortex and Mimir have already introduced the concept of a "namespace" that group one or more alert groups regardless of what file contained those groups. For backwards compatibility the namespace would be the file name if it's not explicitly specified. ## Additional endpoints The following additional endpoints are proposed; the "list" endpoints don't include any expanded fields – "detail" endpoints contain 1 level of expanded fields. ### Files ### List of namespaces `/api/v1/namespaces` Where namespaces are sorted lexographically by `name`.
Response 

{
	"status": "success",
	"data": [{ 
      "name": "my-namespace",
	  "file": "/etc/prometheus/alerts.yml"
	 },
	 { 
	   "name": "another-namespace",
	   "file": "/etc/prometheus/alerts.yml"
	 },
	 { 
	   "name": "third-namespace",
	   "file": "/etc/prometheus/more-alerts.yml"
	 }
	]  
}
#### Single file and its groups `/api/v1/namespaces/:namespace` Where `groups` are sorted lexographically by `name`.
Response 

{
	"status": "success",
	"data": {
	  "name": "my-namespace",
	  "file": "/etc/prometheus/alerts.yml",
	  "groups": [{
	    "name": "My Group",
	    "group_id": "d753f0ded6939ab8f0397f02c717c8839a649200",
	    "file": "/etc/prometheus/alerts.yml",
	    "rules": [],
	    "interval": 0,
	    "limit": 0,
	    "evaluationTime": 0.002,
	    "lastEvaluation": "1970-01-01T00:00:00Z"
	  }, {...}]
	}
}
### Groups #### List of groups `/api/v1/groups` Where groups are sorted by `file` first, and `group name` second. The same as `/api/v1/rules` but with no rules for each group in the response.
Response 

{
	"status": "success",
	"data": {
	  "groups": [
	    {
	      "name": "My Group",
	      "group_id": "d753f0ded6939ab8f0397f02c717c8839a649200",
"namespace": "my-namespace",
	      "file": "/etc/prometheus/alerts.yml",
	    }, 
	    {...}
        ]
    }
}
#### Single group and its rules `/api/v1/groups/:group_identifier` Both return details for a single group and its rules where `rules` are sorted by `state` (`Active > Pending > Inactive`) and then lexographically by `name`.
Response 

{
	"status": "success",
	"data": {
	  "name": "My Group",
	  "group_id": "d753f0ded6939ab8f0397f02c717c8839a649200",
	  "namespace": "my-namespace",
	  "file": "/etc/prometheus/alerts.yml",
	  "rules": [...],
	}
}
### Alert rules #### List of alert rules `/api/v1/rules/status` lexographically sorted by `name`. This would be a list of alert rules, without instances and includes the group and file information.
Response 

{
	"status": "success",
	"data": [
		{
		  "state": "firing",
		  "file": "/etc/prometheus/alerts.yml",
		  "namespace": "my-namespace",
		  "group": "My Group",
		  "group_id": "d753f0ded6939ab8f0397f02c717c8839a649200",
		  "name": "AppCrash",
		  "query": "process_open_fds > 0",
		  "duration": 15,
		  "labels": {
		    "severity": "critical"
		  },
		  "annotations": {
		    "description": "Just testing",
		    "summary": "Number of open fds > 0"
		  },
     }, {...}]
   }
#### Single rule and its alerts `/api/v1/rules/:rule_identifier` Returns the details of a single alert rule and its instances. Sorting instances by `state` (`Active > Pending > Inactive`) then `name`.
Response 

{
	"status": "success",
	"data": {
	  "state": "firing",
	  "file": "/etc/prometheus/alerts.yml",
	  "namespace": "my-namespace",
	  "group": "My Group",
	  "group_id": "d753f0ded6939ab8f0397f02c717c8839a649200",
	  "name": "AppCrash",
	  "query": "process_open_fds > 0",
	  "duration": 15,
	  "labels": {
	    "severity": "critical"
	  },
	  "alerts": [
		{
		  "labels": {
		    "alertname": "AppCrash",
		    "instance": "localhost:9090",
		    "job": "prometheus",
		    "severity": "critical"
		  },
		  "annotations": {
		    "description": "Just testing",
		    "summary": "Number of open fds > 0"
		  },
		  "state": "firing",
		  "activeAt": "2023-04-28T09:01:53.856072543Z",
		  "value": "2.2e+01"
		},
		{...}
           ],
	  "annotations": {
	    "description": "Just testing",
	    "summary": "Number of open fds > 0"
	  },
      }
   }
# Future work ## Updating the Prometheus UI To take full advantage of the new API endpoints we should update the Prometheus UI to use them, this should allow for visualizing large alerting setups. I'm more than willing to put in the work here to make changes to the Prometheus UI if need be. ## Expanding entities Might be worth to explore allowing including or excluding nested resources in the future for the "list" pages. ### Pagination Pagination can be applied to each API endpoint using an implementation discussed in another proposal (unique identifiers are required for pagination with `tokens`). This would further reduce the payload size and allow progressively loading more data to accomodate for really large alert setups. Lots of use-cases can be accomodated if pagination with tokens was implemented on each API endpoint – clients could implement auto-pagination to do filtering and searching on the front-end by simply going through all of the pages. ## Filtering / searching Similar to pagination this can be discussed separately; out of scope for now. ## Special considerations Identifiers should try to avoid using the characters `/` or `\` since [some proxies](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/api-v3/extensions/filters/network/http_connection_manager/v3/http_connection_manager.proto#envoy-v3-api-field-extensions-filters-network-http-connection-manager-v3-httpconnectionmanager-path-with-escaped-slashes-action) don't play nice with those.

### Proposal

TSDB status API https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/querying/api/#tsdb-stats returns various cardinality statistics.
https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/11945 `topN` param got added to return more info we need (default is 10).

However, if users want to check the cardinality of a specifc target or job, if it is not at high cardinality we cannot include those information in response.

The proposal is to add `match[]=<series_selector>` param similar to the GetSeries API and we can look at cardinality of specific series/jobs.
title: Add match[] param to /api/v1/status/tsdb API

### Proposal

The PVE platform is one of the most popular KVM platforms for multiple OS like Linux, Windows, etc. FYI https://pve.proxmox.com/wiki/Main_Page

We can support service discovery for this platform. 

I propose to add `pve_sd_config` field in configuration file like below.

```yaml
pve_sd_config:
  api_endpoint_address: "endpoint for pve server"
  api_endpoint_port: "endpoint port for pve server"
  api_endpoint_user: "user for pve server"
  api_endpoint_password: "password for pve server"
  api_ssl_verify: "verify ssl certificate, bool"
  api_timeout: "timeout for api requests, int"
  api_ssl_pem: "path to ssl pem file"
  exclude_vms: "list of vms to exclude from monitoring"
  include_vms: "list of vms to include in monitoring"
```

If this proposal has been accepted, I would like to take handle to maintain the code and PR

body_text:
### Proposal

Currently, /api/v1/read:

- Writes each series into separate frames. Initially it was done, I think, to have full streaming from Thanos Sidecar perspective but this isn't good for throughput, especially with instant queries. With instant queries, the labels data dominates and there are many series. As a result, most `write()`s write ~1KB. It's more efficient to write fewer but bigger responses. I have tested with `thanosbench` that with bigger queries locally I can reach around 100MB/s throughput whereas with a bunch of smaller responses, I get around 30MB/s.

- Writes each label individually as a string. This means that a lot of data is duplicated in the traffic. Typically, different time series are only different by a few labels. All of the others are the same. I suggest compressing different labels into a symbol table. I am implementing a similar idea in Thanos here: https://github.com/thanos-io/thanos/pull/5906. Yes, this hinders the streaming use case but as far as I can tell we are not opting to have a fully streamable PromQL engine either way. In my experiments in prod, I have seen reductions up to 10x in the amount of network traffic. A similar idea has been implemented in Parca: https://github.com/parca-dev/parca/pull/1976. I think the benefits hugely outweigh the negatives.

With all of that in mind, I suggest implementing a new response type for `/api/v1/read`. Perhaps it could be called `COMPRESSED_XOR`. What do you think?
title: Consider v2 of /api/v1/read with improvements

### What did you do?

We have 4 prom-agents having scrape config as below
regrex is different for each agent(0, 1, 2, and 3)


`      - job_name: 'kube-pods'

        kubernetes_sd_configs:
          - role: pod

        relabel_configs:
          - source_labels: [__address__]
            modulus: 4
            target_label: __tmp_hash
            action: hashmod
          - source_labels: [__tmp_hash]
            regex: ^0$
            action: keep
          - source_labels: [__meta_kubernetes_pod_annotation_prometheus_io_scrape]
            action: keep
            regex: true
          - source_labels: [__meta_kubernetes_pod_annotation_prometheus_io_path]
            action: replace
            target_label: __metrics_path__
            regex: (.+)
          - source_labels: [__address__, __meta_kubernetes_pod_annotation_prometheus_io_port]
            action: replace
            regex: ([^:]+)(?::\d+)?;(\d+)
            replacement: $1:$2
            target_label: __address__
          - action: labelmap
            regex: __meta_kubernetes_pod_label_(.+)
          - source_labels: [__meta_kubernetes_namespace]
            action: replace
            target_label: kubernetes_namespace
          - source_labels: [__meta_kubernetes_pod_name]

our expectations was same metrics should not be scraped by 2 prometheus agent,  which is not working and we are seeing same metrics being scraped by more than 1 agents.

there are some metrics with exactly 1 count as well which means issue is not consistent for all metrics. not sure if its something to do with pods or their config or somethings else.

body_text:
### Proposal

We are monitoring hundreds of Kubernetes clusters from some central observability clusters. To decide whether a cluster is operating fine, relying on current service discovery information seems a reasonable idea -- if we cannot update service discovery information, we definitely have issues with this cluster.

Currently, there are no reasonably usable metrics for this. As we're monitoring across the network, _some_ HTTP errors during service discovery are kind of expected, and just indicate issues after all -- for Prometheus service discovery, we don't mind some errors, but care about whether service discovery works _often enough_ to have a current state. So monitoring based on `prometheus_sd_kubernetes_http_request_total` doesn't work out too well.

There is also `prometheus_sd_updates_total`, but on one hand this is aggregated over all service discovery targets (and a rate still going up even if API server is down), on the other hand it's also just a kind of indirect observation.

I could well imagine all kinds of service discovery should be able to provide a timestamp of the last service discovery update, so a generic alert on failing service discovery for 15 minutes is as easy as `time() - prometheus_sd_last_update > 300`. This metric should be _per service discovery_ configuration block. From a very first peak at the code, this might easily be implemented centrally in `discovery/manager.go` in the update handling code.

<sup>Jens Erat <jens.erat@mercedes-benz.com>, Mercedes-Benz Tech Innovation GmbH, [imprint](https://github.com/mercedes-benz/foss/blob/master/PROVIDER_INFORMATION.md)</sup>
title: Metrics for service discovery latency/age of discovered targets

Nushell has a lot of tests that use the `nu!` macro in unnecessarily complicated ways. For example: https://github.com/nushell/nushell/blob/ed0fce9aa62e9705c3b6c65f9c806f73fb8d6506/crates/nu-command/tests/commands/get.rs#L221

1. `cwd` specifies the working directory to run the test in; this is only useful if the test is performing file I/O. 
2. [The `pipeline()` function](https://github.com/nushell/nushell/blob/ed0fce9aa62e9705c3b6c65f9c806f73fb8d6506/crates/nu-test-support/src/lib.rs#L30) is also not necessary; I believe its main purpose is to let test authors spread a long pipeline across multiple lines to aid readability.
3. The `r#` raw string literal syntax is unnecessary when there are no special characters that need quoting.

The same test could be written like this instead:
```rust
let actual = nu!("[] | get 3");
```

We would welcome contributions to help simplify the tests. A PR that cleans up 1 test would probably be a little too granular. A PR that cleans up several tests in a given area would be good.
title: Tests: clean up unnecessary use of `cwd`, `pipeline()`, etc.

- [ ] [Coming from CMD](https://www.nushell.sh/book/coming_from_cmd.html)

- [ ] [Nu Map from Functional Languages](https://www.nushell.sh/book/nushell_map_functional.html#nu-map-from-functional-languages)

body_text:
### Related problem

While [it's been established](https://github.com/nushell/nushell/issues/11430#issuecomment-1870443444) that `into sqlite`'s ability to *append* to a database is more a "side-effect" than part of its design, it seems so much simpler than `stor insert`.  For example, with a REST call that returns a JSON `items` with a list of records (i.e. a Nu table):

With `into sqlite`:

```Nushell
let res = (http get $endpoint)
$res.items
    | select colname1? colname2? colname5?
    | into sqlite foo.sqlite
```

This currently works when both creating the database as well as updating, as long as the values match their original positions.

With `stor insert`:

```Nushell
let res = (http get $endpoint)
$res.items
    | each {
        |item|
        stor insert -t main -d {
            colname1: $item.colname1,
            colname2: $item.colname2,
            colname5: $item.colname5
        }
    }
```

(^ from memory - Hope I got those right)

### Related problem

Some commands (such as the `into` commands) can update specific cells if cell paths are specified after the command body. `update cells` has a similar behavior, but selects these cells with a `--columns` flag instead of rest arguments.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Change columns flag of `update cells` into a rest argument. For example:

```nushell
[[name val1 val2]; [foo 1 4] [bar 8 3]] | update cells -c [val1 val2] { $in * 2 }
# => ╭───┬──────┬──────┬──────╮
# => │ # │ name │ val1 │ val2 │
# => ├───┼──────┼──────┼──────┤
# => │ 0 │ foo  │    2 │    8 │
# => │ 1 │ bar  │   16 │    6 │
# => ╰───┴──────┴──────┴──────╯
```

is changed to:

```nushell
[[name val1 val2]; [foo 1 4] [bar 8 3]] | update cells { $in * 2 } val1 val2
# => ╭───┬──────┬──────┬──────╮
# => │ # │ name │ val1 │ val2 │
# => ├───┼──────┼──────┼──────┤
# => │ 0 │ foo  │    2 │    8 │
# => │ 1 │ bar  │   16 │    6 │
# => ╰───┴──────┴──────┴──────╯
```

The `--columns` flag should be deprecated, and eventually removed.

_No response_

### Related problem

https://github.com/nushell/nushell/pull/9499 added the possibility to run certain built-in commands at parse time. Adding a support for parse-time evaluation for a command requires a few steps, so the PR added only a few of them. We can now start adding this possibility to more of Nushell's commands.

### How do I add const support to an existing command?

See https://github.com/nushell/nushell/pull/9499 for a short few-step guide

### Which commands can be evaluated at parse time?

Again, see https://github.com/nushell/nushell/pull/9499. We're aiming to port only simple commands that do not read/write files or $env, or have any other side effects (at least for now).

### Describe the solution you'd like

Add the option for more commands to be evaluatable at parse time.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

N/A

### Additional context and details

Since this can potentially be a decent amount of work, we welcome contributors to help us to port the commands. Before submitting a PR, it's better to check with the core team on Discord or in this issue if the commands you'd like to port are intended to be ported, or not. Just to avoid any misunderstandings and potentially wasted work.
title: Allow parse-time evaluation of more commands

We are using the [`uutils/coreutils`](https://github.com/uutils/coreutils) crates for some of our key file-system commands.

Their project has some core crates like  `uucore` and then a series of crates each implementing one of the commands like `uu_mv`. Currently those crates themselves also implement the necessary argument parsing using `clap` which makes sense to create their standalone binaries.
In our usage we only pass arguments as data to the underlying implementation to run the logic while we provide our own arguments parsing and validation.
To do this several people graciously made changes upstream in the architecture for us to have modular access to uutils functionality.

A cherry on top would be if the `clap` implementations would be part of some compile time feature enabled by default for the coreutils project and disabled in our use so we don't have to compile clap and its dependencies and throw everything away at linktime.

## Problem 
We currently have a number of dependencies for which we pull in different versions of the same crate as dependencies in our `cargo tree` have conflicting semver requirements. This causes multiple compilation runs, slows down linking, and causes binary bloat. 

This is on top of crates that functionally duplicate the solution to the same problem (e.g. multiple crates responsible for ANSI coloring or wrappers around the system e.g. for libc or windows system calls)

## Aims
As a first goal we should strive to reduce this version duplication by taking a hard look at dependencies or semver-specs in our crates that cause them.\nEither we eliminate them, choose better versions on our side (as long as this doesn't preclude important bugfixes), or be good stewards and try to contribute upstream version bumps.

title: Reduce accidental dependency duplication

body_text:
### Describe the bug

```
ls | glob '<[!.]*/>[!.]*'
```

will recursively list files but ignore dot-files/dirs

but

```
▶ watch . -v --glob=<[!.]*/>[!.]* { |op, path, new_path| $"($op) ($path) ($new_path)"}
Absolute glob path: "/home/cole/code/nixcfg/<[!.]*/>[!.]*"
```

body_text:
### Related problem

Quite often (especially in testing the engine-q changes), panics occur - forcefully exiting the shell and closing whatever tab it was in (if exec or default shell was used to start it).

This is a horrible user experience for bugs related to completion or highlighting or other non-critical shell related features that could have reasonable fallbacks. In general rust standards advise panics be the absolute last resort for unrecoverable errors - and I don't think highlighting or completion fall (and even some lexer issues related to aliases) fall under unrecoverable.

### Describe the solution you'd like

I'm proposing the removal of all or most panics (priority being on completion or highlighting first). I currently count 74 uses of panic as of fbaafaa4.

While certain panics are obviously not recoverable, I believe any of the ones in the completion or highlighting should be able to just fail with no completion or highlighting being done.

I think many of the panics are around incorrect spans and lexer parsing, and I would rather the CLI show incorrect characters, highlighting, or other odd behavior rather than having the shell forcefully exit on me - leaving me no options to backspace or recover.

I'm open to ideas around making this experience better if the above isn't the correct approach, and additional ideas around logging or error reporting in these cases would be helpful so that errors aren't just swallowed (and thus unreported)

### Describe alternatives you've considered

I'm wondering if it's possible to refactor some of the panic cases into Results instead, allowing the highest level caller to handle them more gracefully such as disabling highlighting, reverting to functionality for an unrecognized command/syntax shape, etc.

### Additional context and details

body_text:
### Related problem

There were a sequence of subtle bugs and slightly broken releases relating to pipeline management and signal handling (see https://github.com/nushell/nushell/pull/6542 for a summary). It is looking like https://github.com/nushell/nushell/pull/6584 fixes the known issues, and it would be valuable to have tests preventing future regressions. @unrelentingtech suggests (https://github.com/nushell/nushell/pull/6584#issuecomment-1252425494) that this might follow the [patterns used by fish](https://github.com/fish-shell/fish-shell/tree/master/tests/pexpects) to implement similar tests, which use the [pexpect](https://pexpect.readthedocs.io/en/stable/) tool:

https://github.com/fish-shell/fish-shell/tree/master/tests/pexpects

### Describe the solution you'd like

Tests that prevent regressions relating to pipelines and signal handling. Ideally, it should be possible to cherry-pick the tests onto some past commits and verify that the tests fail on  commits with the bugs described in https://github.com/nushell/nushell/pull/6542 (e.g. #6240 and #6496).

### Describe alternatives you've considered

I don't see an alternative; nushell should have such tests at some point.

Errors that do not have spans are not very useful because they do not point at where the error happened. Example is `ShellError::IOError`. Maybe we should modify all error types to require a span and pass `call.head` to it as a bare minimum. There might be exceptions where this is not possible but in general I would strive to require spans on as many error types as possible.

Related: nushell/nushell#4326
title: Deprecate error types without spans

body_text:
## Summary

`return $x` throws away any pipeline metadata attached to `$x`. The same value returned in tail position keeps it.

This looks like a by-product of early return riding the `ShellError` unwind chain: the unwound value is a bare `Value`, and pipeline metadata lives on `PipelineData`, so it is dropped on the way out.

## Reproduce

```nushell
def tail-return  [] { "body" | metadata set { merge {"my.meta": {status: 302}} } }
def early-return [] { if true { return ("body" | metadata set { merge {"my.meta": {status: 302}} }) } }

print ("tail-return:  " + (tail-return  | metadata | get -o "my.meta" | to nuon))
print ("early-return: " + (early-return | metadata | get -o "my.meta" | to nuon))
```

Output:

```
tail-return:  {status: 302}
early-return: null
```

## Expected

`early-return` preserves the metadata, matching `tail-return`.

## Why it happens

Tracing the two return paths through the IR evaluator.

The block's implicit final return hands the register back whole ([`eval_ir.rs:1024`](https://github.com/nushell/nushell/blob/main/crates/nu-engine/src/eval_ir.rs#L1024)):

```rust
Instruction::Return { src } => Ok(Return(*src)),   // -> take_reg -> full PipelineData
```

The `return` keyword compiles to `ReturnEarly`, which collects the register into a `Value` ([`eval_ir.rs:1017`](https://github.com/nushell/nushell/blob/main/crates/nu-engine/src/eval_ir.rs#L1017)):

```rust
Instruction::ReturnEarly { src } => {
    let val = ctx.collect_reg(*src, *span)?;        // into_value() drops metadata
    Err(ShellError::Return { span: *span, value: Box::new(val) })
}
```

The `ShellError::Return` variant carries only that `Value` ([`shell_error/mod.rs:1178`](https://github.com/nushell/nushell/blob/main/crates/nu-protocol/src/errors/shell_error/mod.rs#L1178)):

```rust
Return { span: Span, value: Box<Value> },
```

At the catch site it becomes a `PipelineData` with metadata `None` ([`eval.rs:523`](https://github.com/nushell/nushell/blob/main/crates/nu-engine/src/eval.rs#L523)):

```rust
Err(ShellError::Return { span: _, value }) =>
    Ok(PipelineExecutionData::from(PipelineData::value(*value, None))),
```

## Impact

[http-nu](https://github.com/cablehead/http-nu), an HTTP server scripted in Nushell, sets a response's status and headers via [`http.response` pipeline metadata](https://github.com/cablehead/http-nu#response-metadata) (the `custom` metadata from #16821). A handler builds its response as a value tagged with that metadata. Returning it with `return` drops the tag, so the response is sent with the default status 200 instead of the redirect the handler set. The value still comes back, so the handler looks like it worked.

## Possible directions

1. Add a `metadata: Option<PipelineMetadata>` field to `ShellError::Return`. Grab the metadata before collapsing to `Value`, and put it back at the catch site. `Value` stays as it is; the metadata rides the error, not the value. Small change. A live stream still collapses to a `Value`, but the metadata survives.
2. Route explicit `return` through the same path as the implicit tail return, so it carries the full `PipelineData`. Bigger change: today the error channel handles `try`/`finally` unwinding, and a non-error path would need to do that itself.

## Configuration

- Nushell 0.113.1 (also confirmed unchanged on `main` at 6e9105d88, 0.114 dev)
title: `return` silently drops pipeline metadata

### Related problem

Related: https://github.com/nushell/nushell/issues/5803

I'm wanting to try using nushell to develop on Windows.  However, I currently use Microsoft's BATCH scripts (i.e. `vcvarsall.bat` or `VsDevCmd.bat`) to initialize environment variables in order to make the current shell a "Visual Studio Command Prompt".  Since this is Microsofts chosen interface, it's common for other projects to provide the same interface for initializing environment variables via BATCH files as well.  I'd like to be able to leverage this interface inside NuShell.

### Describe the solution you'd like

A new builtin command to run a batch file, provide it command line arguments and import it's environment variables into the current environment.  Here's what that might look like:

```nushell
# runs the batch script and imports it's environment variables
source vsvarsall.bat --arch=amd64
```


### Describe alternatives you've considered

One solution to this is to start a session via `CMD.exe`, execute the BATCH scripts, and then start your nu process from that CMD.exe environment.  This should work but is more cumbersome and also means you couldn't leverage nu features like overlays to manage the environment.

There also is currently a nuscript that attempts to re-implement one or more of Microsoft's BATCH scripts that initialize the environment here: https://github.com/nushell/nu_scripts/blob/main/modules/virtual_environments/nu_msvs/nu_msvs.nu

However, Microsoft drastically changes it's BATCH scripts across versions and this also means any project that also leverages the same interface will also have to rewrite their scripts in nu.

### Additional context and details

I created a crude proof of concept nushell script that could accomplish this task in specific cases.

```nushell
def-env sourcebat [...cmd: string] {
  let cmd = ($cmd | append ["&&" echo "___ENV_FOR_NUSHELL___" "&&" set])
  let result = do { cmd.exe /c $cmd } | complete
  let offset = $result.stdout | str index-of "___ENV_FOR_NUSHELL__"
  if $offset == -1 {
    print $result.stdout
    print $result.stderr
    return $result.exit_code
  }
  print ($result.stdout | str substring 0..$offset)
  print $result.stderr

  let offset = $offset + 20
  let batenv = $result.stdout | str substring $offset.. | split row "\n"

  for line in $batenv {
    let eq_index = $line | str index-of "="
    if $eq_index == -1 { continue }
    let name = $line | str substring ..$eq_index
    let value_start = $eq_index + 1      
    let value = $line | str substring $value_start..
    print $"Setting ($name) to ($value)"
    if $name != PWD and $name != CURRENT_FILE and $name != FILE_PWD {
      load-env { $name: $value }
    }
  }
}
```

It passes the input command-line to CMD.exe and appends the following to the command which will cause it to dump a marker and then the full environment: `&& echo __ENV_FOR_NULSHELL__ && set`.  The nu script can then parse the output and export the environment variables to the caller.    However this is brittle and has bugs (i.e. doesn't remove variables, messes up env conversions, etc), a better solution would be to not capture stdout/stderr in the child CMD.exe process and instead append a command that passes the resulting environment variables back to the NuShell process through a side-channel (i.e. named pipe maybe).  I think this should be builtin, but internally it could be doing something like this:

```batch
cmd /c "forward whatever command we got from the user && nu -send-env-to MY_NAMED_PIPE"
```

This `nu -send-env-to MY_NAMED_PIPE` would send it's current environment to the parent nu process, in this case it's going through a named pipe but maybe there are better methods I'm not aware of.
title: import environment variables from batch scripts on Windows

### Describe the bug

This is a follow-up for #13072, which fixed a more general issue where `OneOf` did not work at all (never matched anything) for named arguments. That problem was indeed fixed in the latest release, but apparently it doesn't work for all types - specifically it does not work for blocks.

### How to reproduce

1. Use the following `Cargo.toml`:
    ```rust
    [package]
    name = "nu_plugin_example"
    version = "0.1.0"
    edition = "2021"

    [dependencies]
    nu-plugin = "0.97.1"
    nu-protocol = { version = "0.97.1", features = ["plugin"] }
    ```
2. Use the following `main.rs`:
    ```rust
    use nu_plugin::{
        serve_plugin, EngineInterface, EvaluatedCall, MsgPackSerializer, Plugin, PluginCommand,
    };
    use nu_protocol::{LabeledError, PipelineData, Signature, SyntaxShape};

    struct ExamplePlugin;

    impl Plugin for ExamplePlugin {
        fn commands(&self) -> Vec<Box<dyn PluginCommand<Plugin = Self>>> {
            vec![Box::new(ExampleCommand)]
        }

        fn version(&self) -> String {
            env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION").to_owned()
        }
    }

    struct ExampleCommand;

    impl PluginCommand for ExampleCommand {
        type Plugin = ExamplePlugin;

        fn name(&self) -> &str {
            "example"
        }

        fn signature(&self) -> Signature {
            Signature::new("example")
                .named("foo", SyntaxShape::Block, "", None)
                .named("bar", SyntaxShape::Closure(None), "", None)
                .named(
                    "baz",
                    SyntaxShape::OneOf(vec![SyntaxShape::Block, SyntaxShape::Closure(None)]),
                    "",
                    None,
                )
                .optional(
                    "positional",
                    SyntaxShape::OneOf(vec![SyntaxShape::Block, SyntaxShape::Closure(None)]),
                    "",
                )
        }

        fn usage(&self) -> &str {
            ""
        }

        fn run(
            &self,
            _plugin: &Self::Plugin,
            _engine: &EngineInterface,
            _call: &EvaluatedCall,
            _input: PipelineData,
        ) -> Result<PipelineData, LabeledError> {
            Ok(PipelineData::empty())
        }
    }

    fn main() {
        serve_plugin(&ExamplePlugin, MsgPackSerializer);
    }
    ```
    Note that I added both `SyntaxShape::Block`, `SyntaxShape::Closure(None)` - they should both match against blocks, but for some reason none of them does. Even if I only use one of them it doesn't work.
3. `cargo build`
4. `nu --plugins '[target/debug/nu_plugin_example]'`
5. In the created shell:
    * For `--foo` and `--bar`, which don't use `OneOf`, it works without issues:
        ```nushell
        > example --foo {}
        > example --foo {|| ls}
        > example --foo {ls}
        > example --bar {}
        > example --bar {|| ls}
        > example --bar {ls}
        ```
    * For positional arguments it also works without issue:
        ```nushell
        > example {}
        > example {|| ls}
        > example {ls}
        ```
    * For `--baz`, which does use `OneOf`, it works for empty blocks and for blocks with an argument list:
        ```nushell
        > example --baz {}
        > example --baz {|| ls}
        ```
    * But blocks without argumnet list don't work for `--baz`:
        ```nushell
        > example --baz {ls}
        Error: nu::parser::parse_mismatch_with_full_string_msg

          × Parse mismatch during operation.
           ╭─[entry #12:1:15]
         1 │ example --baz {ls}
           ·               ──┬─
           ·                 ╰── expected non-block value: one_of(block, closure())
           ╰────

        ```

### Expected behavior

It should work for `--baz` the same way it works for positional arguments.

Also - the very error message demonstrates the issue:
```
expected non-block value: one_of(block, closure())
```
If `block` is one of the `one_of` options, it should not be expecting "non-block" values.

### Screenshots

```nushell
> nu --plugins '[target/debug/nu_plugin_example]' --commands 'example --baz {ls}'
Error: nu::parser::parse_mismatch_with_full_string_msg

  × Parse mismatch during operation.
   ╭─[source:1:15]
 1 │ example --baz {ls}
   ·               ──┬─
   ·                 ╰── expected non-block value: one_of(block, closure())
   ╰────
```

### Configuration

```nushell
| key                | value                                                            |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| version            | 0.97.1                                                           |
| major              | 0                                                                |
| minor              | 97                                                               |
| patch              | 1                                                                |
| branch             | makepkg                                                          |
| commit_hash        | 60769ac1ba3ea036d889f140095d855e5597840c                         |
| build_os           | linux-x86_64                                                     |
| build_target       | x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu                                         |
| rust_version       | rustc 1.80.1 (3f5fd8dd4 2024-08-06) (Arch Linux rust 1:1.80.1-1) |
| cargo_version      | cargo 1.80.1 (376290515 2024-07-16)                              |
| build_time         | 2024-08-21 12:14:01 +00:00                                       |
| build_rust_channel | release                                                          |
| allocator          | mimalloc                                                         |
| features           | default, sqlite, system-clipboard, trash                         |
| installed_plugins  | skim 0.4.0                                                       |
```

### Additional context

My actual usecase is
```rust
SyntaxShape::OneOf(vec![
    SyntaxShape::CellPath,
    SyntaxShape::Closure(Some(vec![])),
])
```
I want this for the `--format` and `--preview` fields of [`nu_plugin_skim`](https://github.com/idanarye/nu_plugin_skim). If the user enters a closure the value will be formatted using that closure, but if they entered a cell path I'd use the cell path to extract the data from the value.

This meas that, for example, instead of
```nushell
ls | sk --format {get name}
```

One could simply write
```nushell
ls | sk --format name
```
title: `SyntaxShape::OneOf` does not support blocks (closures without arguments) for named arguments

body_text:
Implementing `Copy` for iterators makes footguns, and [the standard library settled not to do so](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/21846#issuecomment-110526401) for now.

```rust
let mut it = /* a Copy + Iterator */;
for x in it { if cond { break; } } // `it` copied here (forgot to `&mut it`)
let x = it.next(); // `it` is in the initial state
```

Clippy should have a lint that warns if "use of the original iterator after copied" is detected.
title: Lint for Iterator + Copy

body_text:
clippy warns if one tries to use a type like `Rc<Vec<T>>`, e.g.

```
Arc<Vec<u8>>
^^^^^^^^^^^^ help: try: `Arc<[u8]>`
```

This is dangerous as creating a `Rc<[T]>` causes a `memcpy` of the whole memory area with all the elements, while creating an `Rc<Vec<T>>` simply copies over the 3 pointers inside the `Vec` without copying all the elements.

A better suggestion would probably be `Rc<Box<[T]>>` as that has the same runtime behaviour, but even independent of that it can be useful to have a `Vec` inside an `Rc` / `Arc` in combination with the `make_mut()` / `get_mut()` API.

The lint should probably be at least disabled by default.

----

The same also applies to `Rc<String>` vs `Rc<str>`.

Based on [this HIC++ guideline](http://www.codingstandard.com/rule/5-2-2-ensure-that-functions-do-not-call-themselves-either-directly-or-indirectly/).

The stack explodes much faster using recursion than a huge BFS work queue would explode the heap. Therefore, if clippy detects some direct or indirect recursion that does not benefit from tail call optimisation, clippy should issue a warning along with a short description about why this is potentially bad and a short hint on how to transform recursive algorithms to iterative ones *(e.g. using a work queue and BFS)*. And maybe a tl;dr about what tail calls are and how to make the algorithm tail recursive.

body_text:
### What it does

Inspired by this code in the standard library: https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/std/collections/hash/set.rs.html#864-866
```rust
    pub fn is_subset(&self, other: &HashSet<T, S>) -> bool {
        if self.len() <= other.len() { self.iter().all(|v| other.contains(v)) } else { false }
    }
```
which could instead be 
```rust
    pub fn is_subset(&self, other: &HashSet<T, S>) -> bool {
        self.len() <= other.len() && self.iter().all(|v| other.contains(v))
    }
```

When the "then" block is a single simple expression (rather than a complex thing with a bunch of `let`s, say), seeing `else { false }` is a hint that the code can be simplified without changing behaviour or performance.

Playground repro that this is not linted today: <https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=nightly&mode=debug&edition=2024&gist=90c86a06c5fce6c0f816f5f4ec170cc5>

---

Similarly, suggesting `A || B` instead of `if A { true } else { B }` would also be good.

### Advantage

- Shorter and arguably simpler code
- Makes it clearer that this is an "and"
  - By having things that are just `&&`s *be* `&&`s it helps emphasize the places that *do* need the `if`-`else` for their less-common operation.

### Drawbacks

If either condition is particularly complicated, splitting it up into the two pieces might help a reader grok the intent.

### Example

```rust
    pub fn is_subset(&self, other: &HashSet<T, S>) -> bool {
        if self.len() <= other.len() { self.iter().all(|v| other.contains(v)) } else { false }
    }
```
Could be written as:
```rust
    pub fn is_subset(&self, other: &HashSet<T, S>) -> bool {
        self.len() <= other.len() && self.iter().all(|v| other.contains(v))
    }
```

body_text:
### What it does

I would like clippy to lint against *all* integer casts. So I have set:
```rust
#![warn(
    clippy::cast_possible_wrap, // unsigned -> signed
    clippy::cast_sign_loss, // signed -> unsigned
    clippy::cast_lossless,
    clippy::cast_possible_truncation,
)]
```
However, I just by accident noticed that this does *not* lint against usize-to-u64 casts. I guess `cast_possible_truncation` says "this cannot truncate because we don't have more than 64bit pointer size", and "cast_lossless" says "ah this might be lossy on platforms with pointers larger than 64bit", and then neither of them does anything.

I would be happy to either have one of these lints also trigger on usize-to-u64 casts, or to have a new lint against *all* integer casts.

### Lint Name

cast_integer

### Category

pedantic

### Advantage

Integer casts are subtle and should be done via `From`/`TryFrom`, never via `as`, so I want to rule out *all* of them in my codebase.

### Drawbacks

_No response_

### Example

```rust
pub fn foo(x: usize) -> u64 { x as u64 }
```

Could be written as:

```rust
pub fn foo(x: usize) -> u64 { u64::try_from(x).unwrap() }
```

### What it does

I've noticed [a few places in the code with which I work](https://fuchsia.googlesource.com/fuchsia/+/a6449debce0f67f75c329bda150987ab7a3d15f3%5E%21/#F0) where `Ok(` and `?)` can be removed from the ends of a line without altering system behavior - would it be good to have Clippy flag those?

### Advantage

The advantage would be that the code on the page gets to avoid (a small bit of) unnecessary syntactic structural complexity.

### Drawbacks

_Maybe_ some folks like seeing the `Ok` as a visual reminder or cue of "this is an exit point of the current behavior"? Since there's not a `return` keyword like in other languages? ... but I'm just supposing and speculating about that.

### Example

```rust
Ok(helper_function_call(4)?)
```

Could be written as:

```rust
helper_function_call(4)
```

### Comparison with existing lints

I had figured that this probably already existed, but it doesn't yet seem to, nor did I find any past issue proposing it.

### Additional Context

I'm not aware of any additional context; feel free to inform me about what I am overlooking.
title: How about a `redundant_ok` lint?

### Summary

The lint has a suggestion template for when the array/vec initializer is a part of a `LetStmt`, but in this particular case:
```rs
match 0 {
    0 => _ = [f(); 0],
    _ => {},
}
```
its suggestion:
```
warning: function or method calls as the initial value in zero-sized array initializers may cause side effects
 --> src/lib.rs:9:14
  |
9 |         _ => _ = [f(); 0],
  |              ^^^^^^^^^^^^ help: consider using: `f(); let _: [(); 0] = [];`
  |
```
doesn't work for multiple reasons:
- Despite this being a `Stmt` in a `Block`, it has no surrounding braces, so `f(); _: [(); 0] = [];`, which introduces a second statement, is invalid
- ~The `_: [(); 0] = [];` part won't compile anyway -- the `LetStmt` is lacking a `let`, and so a type ascription is not allowed~
    - ~The following would work though: `_ = [] as [(); 0];`~
- ~Lastly, it adds a `let ` that wasn't there to begin with~

(EDIT: the last two happen on regular `_ = [f(); 0];`s as well, opened a separate issue for that: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust-clippy/issues/15825)

### Reproducer

I tried this code:

```rust
#![allow(unused)]
#![warn(clippy::zero_repeat_side_effects)]

fn f() {}

fn foo() {
    match 0 {
        0 => _ = [f(); 0],
        _ => {},
    }
}
```

This happened:
```
warning: function or method calls as the initial value in zero-sized array initializers may cause side effects
 --> src/lib.rs:9:14
  |
9 |         _ => _ = [f(); 0],
  |              ^^^^^^^^^^^^ help: consider using: `f(); let _: [(); 0] = [];`
  |
```

I expected this to happen:
No suggestion

### Version

```text
rustc 1.90.0 (1159e78c4 2025-09-14)
binary: rustc
commit-hash: 1159e78c4747b02ef996e55082b704c09b970588
commit-date: 2025-09-14
host: x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
release: 1.90.0
LLVM version: 20.1.8
```

### Additional Labels

@rustbot label I-suggestion-causes-error

body_text:
### What it does

This lint warns unintentional large temporary values which may cause an overflowed stack.

Taking this function definition:

```rust
const LENGTH: usize = 1048576;

fn foo(buf: &[u8; LENGTH]) {
    let _a = buf;
}
```

On the signature, a thin ref `&[u8; LENGTH]` ensures the argument passed in should have exactly this size. Out of the function, `array.try_into().unwrap()` can be used as an assertion to the array size. However,

```rust
fn main() {
    let buf = vec![0_u8; LENGTH];
    // No! equivalent to: foo(&<[u8; LENGTH]>::try_from(buf).unwrap())
    foo(&buf.try_into().unwrap());
}
```

One may carelessly write a function call like above (I searched and found many occurrences like this on GitHub). Note, it will create a `[u8; LENGTH]` temporary value that is then referenced and passed to the function. This temporary value may cause an overflowed stack.

In this case above, due to different stack size limit on the two platforms, it runs smoothly on Linux but Stack overflow encounters on Windows. This may be tricky somehow.

### Advantage

- Avoid unneeded stack temporary values and potential stack overflow errors.

### Drawbacks

_No response_

### Example

```rust
let buf: Vec<T> = ...
foo(&buf.try_into().unwrap());
```

Could be written as:

```rust
let buf: Vec<T> = ...
foo(<&[T; LENGTH]>::try_from(&buf[..]).unwrap());
```

Or,
```rust
let buf: Vec<T> = ...
foo((&buf[..]).try_into().unwrap());
```

### Comparison with existing lints

We have [`large_stack_arrays`](https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-clippy/master/index.html#large_stack_arrays) lint but this is unable to detect such cases.

### Additional Context

_No response_
title: Lint for large on-stack temporary values

body_text:
I originally wanted to suggest a new lint which would check the following pattern:
```rust
fn foo(opt: Option<i32>, default: i32) -> i32 {
    opt.map_or(default, |o| o)
}
```

and would rewrite it as:
```rust
fn foo(opt: Option<i32>, default: i32) -> i32 {
    opt.unwrap_or(default)
}
```
and same with `Option::map_or_else`.

But it turns out that there's already a pretty similar lint, [`unnecessary_result_map_or_else`](https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-clippy/master/index.html#unnecessary_result_map_or_else), which does the same for `Result`s. Therefore, I'd instead suggest revamping that lint, by adding support both for `Result::map_or` and `Option::map_or{,_else}`.

That would of course require a name change, and I'd intuitively go with `unnecessary_map_or_else`. But there's already an [`unnecessary_map_or`](https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-clippy/master/index.html#unnecessary_map_or) -- and I kind of feel like this new lint is more deserving of that name; maybe `unnecessary_map_or` could be renamed to something like `map_or_for_partialeq`?..

Also, currently `unnecessary_result_map_or_else` uses some bespoke algorithm to find out whether the "map closure" (as they call it) is an identity closure -- I think we should just switch to `is_expr_untyped_identity_function` instead. I guess this could be done separately from the rest.

### What it does

`wrap_on_overflow` would raise a warning if `wrapping_add` (or similar methods) are invoked.

`saturate_on_overflow` would raise a warning if `saturating_add` (or similar methods) are invoked.

### Advantage

In my work, I regularly control the behavior on overflow, but I prefer using `saturating_*`. Unfortunately, for whatever reason, I continue to accidentally type (and thankfully seem to catch) `wrapping_*`. I'm concerned for the day I write `wrapping_` and DON'T catch it. I also have yet to want, in my repository, wrap on overflow and accordingly am fine banning it entirely (without the `allow` pragma).

I believe a pedantic lint to explicitly declare saturation vs wrap as the preferred way to handle overflow is worthwhile accordingly. This would be approximate to the existing lints establishing preferences on endianess.

### Drawbacks

_No response_

### Example

```rust
a.wrapping_add(b)
```

Could be written as:

```rust
a.saturating_add(b)
```

### Comparison with existing lints

https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-clippy/master/index.html#arithmetic_side_effects already exists to require _a_ mode be specified, but it doesn't allow declaring a preferred mode.

The premise is comparable to https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-clippy/master/index.html#big_endian_bytes, https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-clippy/master/index.html#host_endian_bytes, https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-clippy/master/index.html#little_endian_bytes which allow declaring a preferred mode to represent bytes.

### Additional Context

_No response_
title: `restriction` lints for undesired method of handling overflow

body_text:
### What it does

The lint allows users to forbid using certain types via certain trait interfaces, for instance:

`clippy.toml`:
```toml
disallowed-trait-usage = [
   { type = "std::fs::PathBuf", trait = "std::fmt::Debug", reason = "Use path.display() instead" },
]
```

### Advantage

**My use case**: forbidding using `Debug` formatting of certain types.

I am in constant pursuit of improving error messages across the crate eco-system. An easy (and common) mistake is to use `Debug` formatting `{:?}` when `Display` formatting `{}` would be better, e.g. in log calls and error message formatting. This also applies to GUIs. Usually, if there is a `Display` implementation, that's what should be used in any user-facing code (arguable everywhere outside of `dbg!`).

So I'd like to be able to use `Clippy` to find all these cases, and I think a good way of accomplishing it is to say "I forbid datatype X to be used via the `std::fmt::Debug` trait".

An example of where I've manually searched for `Debug` formatting and replacing it with `Display` (and surely missing many places):
* https://github.com/apache/datafusion/pull/17565

### Example

`clippy.toml`:
```toml
disallowed-trait-usage = [
   { type = "std::fs::PathBuf", trait = "std::fmt::Debug", reason = "Use path.display() instead" },
]
```

```rust
anyhow::bail!("No such file: {path:?}");

// Or:

fn print(x: &dyn Debug) { … }
print(&my_path);
```

->

```
clippy::disallowed-trait-usage: Not allowed to use `std::fs::PathBuf` as trait `std::fmt::Debug`. Reason: "Use path.display() instead"
```

### Comparison with existing lints

There is not existing lint to cover this, but there is a similar suggestion here:
* https://github.com/rust-lang/rust-clippy/issues/8581#issuecomment-3302351887

The difference is that `disallowed-trait-usage` would forbid _all_ trait methods on a type. I suspect this is actually easier to implement in `clippy`.
title: New lint: `disallowed-trait-usage`

body_text:
### What it does

It warns about the issue described [here](https://blog.polybdenum.com/2024/01/17/identifying-the-collect-vec-memory-leak-footgun.html).

TLDR: `v.into_iter()...collect::<Vec<_>>()` can in general be optimized to run in-place and use `v`'s memory. But this means that, for example, `v.into_iter().take(k).collect::<Vec<_>>()` will have `len() = k` and `capacity() = v.len()`. See [playground example](https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2024&gist=194fa11c1f9d27900574684618ab0e7e).

Clippy should warn about such patterns (the degree of generality remains open) and suggest applying `shrink_to_fit` to the result or using different methods of extracting the desired values.

### Advantage

The problematic code may result in unexpectedly high memory usage. The suggested changes (or even just raising awareness about this behavior) would prevent such scenarios.

### Drawbacks

It's difficult to know exactly when the in-place optimization applies, so the user should manually check if the suggested change is needed in their case.

I guess it might be annoying for those who know the internal iterators well and expect this behavior.

### Example

```rust
    let b: Vec<_> = a.into_iter().take(5).collect();
```

Could be written as:

```rust
    let b: Vec<_> = {
        let mut b = a.into_iter().take(5).collect();
        b.shrink_to_fit();
   };
```
Although there are probably better options.

### Comparison with existing lints

_No response_

### Additional Context

_No response_
title: Warn that `v.into_iter().take().collect::<Vec<_>>()` might not release `v`'s memory

I suggesting new way to set up various levels for thresholds, e.g.:
- __forbid__ `large_stack_frames` for `stack-size-threshold = 4096`
- __warn__ `large_stack_frames` for `stack-size-threshold = 2048` <hr/>

- __deny__ `large_stack_arrays` for `array-size-threshold = 32`
- __warn__ `large_stack_arrays` for `array-size-threshold = 16`


It could be configurable in `clippy.toml` like this:
```toml
stack-size-threshold.forbid = 4096
# or
stack-size-threshold = { forbid = 4096, warn = 2048, ... }
# and same for array-size-threshold:
array-size-threshold.deny = 32
array-size-threshold.warn = 16
```

- - -

This issue describes possible improvement for `clippy.toml` size-thresholds configuration.
But because `clippy.toml` works globally for entire "project" (workspace or just crate with multiple different-purposed functions), this suggestioned changes could be highly useful in general, but not in special cases with various stack-sizes and cache-lines.
That's why I'v also create another suggestion (#15735) about a way to specify thresholds precisely for concrete item or scope.
There is also described my motivation for both suggestions.
title: suggestion: Differentiate size-thresholds levels (forbid, deny, warn)

### Describe the Bug

Defining a dataclass with an `InitVar` field causes pyrefly to insist every value assigned to the field to also be `InitVar`. Instead, pyrefly should behave as if `InitVar` were not there, i.e. pyrefly should interpret `mode: InitVar[str]` as `mode: str`.

```
from dataclasses import dataclass, field, InitVar

@dataclass
class Data:
    value: int = field(init=False)
    mode: InitVar[str]

    def __post_init__(self, mode: str):
        if mode == "number":
            self.value = 10
        else:
            self.value = 0

d = Data("number")
```

Result:

```
ERROR 14:10-18: Argument `Literal['number']` is not assignable to parameter `mode` with type `InitVar[str]` in function `Data.__init__` [[bad-argument-type](https://pyrefly.org/en/docs/error-kinds/#bad-argument-type)]
```

body_text:
### Describe the Bug

A `match` arm with a sequence pattern whose element is a **literal** (`case "b", v`) doesn't get subtracted from the union after the `match`. The same code with a **capture** (`case k, v`) narrows to `Never` correctly. (Different from the fixed #3147, which used a wildcard `case (_, _)`.)

```python
from typing import Literal, reveal_type

type MyUnion = Literal["a"] | tuple[Literal["b"], int] | tuple[Literal["c"], int]


def broken(value: MyUnion) -> str:  # Function declared to return `str`, but one or more paths are missing an explicit `return`
    match value:
        case "a":
            return "a"
        case "b", v:
            reveal_type(v)  # revealed type: int
            return "b"
        case "c", v:
            reveal_type(v)  # revealed type: int
            return "c"
    reveal_type(value)  # revealed type: tuple[Literal['b'], int] | tuple[Literal['c'], int]


def works(value: MyUnion) -> str:
    match value:
        case "a":
            return "a"
        case k, v:
            reveal_type(k)  # revealed type: Literal['b', 'c']
            reveal_type(v)  # revealed type: int
            return k
    reveal_type(value)  # revealed type: Never
```

`broken` is exhaustive, so `value` should narrow to `Never` like in `works`, and the `bad-return` is spurious.

`pyrefly` version: 1.1.1

### Describe the Bug

When running pyrefly check on this file: https://github.com/psalvaggio/scientific_pydantic/blob/main/tests/numpy/test_dtype.py#L22

I expect line 22 to be OK, but it actually gives:

```
[Pyrefly] Argument `Literal['>i4']` is not assignable to parameter `dtype` with type `dtype[Any]` in function `DefaultModel.__init__`
```

Background:

This is a library I am working on that has a number of pydantic adapters for scientific types. The one I linked here is for `numpy.dtype`, but the issue is similar on a number of other ones.

The field is annotated like:

```python
dtype: ty.Annotated[np.dtype, DTypeAdapter()]
```

where `DTypeAdapter()` make a custom schema for the `np.dtype`. This particular schema is a plain validator that takes `Any` and either converts to a dtype or raises an exception, resulting in a validation error.

I would expect `pyrefly` to take `Any` for `dtype` in the model constructor, but it instead is constraining to `np.dtype`.

I think if there is a custom type in an `Annotated` field that implements `__get_pydantic_core_schema__`, then `pyrefly` should probably be fairly lax on the constraints for the corresponding keyword argument.

Happy to discuss or provide more details.

body_text:
### Describe the Bug

I'd like autocompletion when constructing anonymous dictionaries in function calls that expect a `TypedDict` as the argument.

For example:

```
from typing import TypedDict


class Box(TypedDict):
    x: float
    y: float
    z: float


def take(box: Box):
    return


take({""})  
    # ^ When the cursor is in this position, there's no autocompletion of the keys in `Box`
```

body_text:
As you know, Python's builtin tokenizer, parse tree, AST, bytecode, stack frames and much more is directly available to use as importable python modules. This has in-turn made it much easier to create tools like `flake8` and `pyupgrade` directly on top of them.

It would be very helpful to keep a similar spirit in mind when developing `pyrefly`, both as a Rust crate and as a Python package, providing for eg. direct Python functions to be able to extract full/partial import graphs, data flow graphs, generated SSA, inferred types etc. as directly accessible Python objects. It helps other tools very easily extend the core functionality provided by the package in ways that would fall completely out of the scope of this project, but nevertheless use the exact same base tools.

A good example would be writing an optimizer: having strictly checked type information available programmatically can help write automations to inline certain functions, replace loops with comprehensions, and other such changes with complete confidence in the runtime behaviour not changing.

Another example would be automatically finding and deleting dead code in an application codebase, based on which functions are referenced within the codebase and which simply aren't.
title: Planning around usage as a library

body_text:
### Describe the Bug

You can assign me to this, I will PR.

This issue talks about `match await ...` because that's how I noticed it, but also happens without await.

Pyrefly reports `bad-return` for an exhaustive `match await ...` statement, but accepts the equivalent code when the awaited result is first assigned to a local variable and then matched.
This affects common async code that matches on a result-like union.
### Repro
```python
from typing import NoReturn
class Ok[T]:
    __match_args__ = ("value",)
    value: T
class Err[E]:
    __match_args__ = ("value",)
    value: E
class NotFound:
    pass
def handle_error(error: NotFound) -> NoReturn:
    raise Exception()
async def get_result() -> Ok[list[int]] | Err[NotFound]:
    raise Exception()
async def f_match_await() -> list[int]:
    match await get_result():
        case Ok(value):
            return value
        case Err(error):
            handle_error(error)
async def f_assign_then_match() -> list[int]:
    result = await get_result()
    match result:
        case Ok(value):
            return value
        case Err(error):
            handle_error(error)
```
### Actual Behavior
Pyrefly reports:
```text
ERROR Function declared to return `list[int]`, but one or more paths are missing an explicit `return` [bad-return]
```
on `f_match_await`.
`f_assign_then_match` passes.
### Expected Behavior
Both functions should be accepted. `match await get_result()` should have the same exhaustiveness behavior as:
```python
result = await get_result()
match result:
    ...
```

Likely root cause: `match await ...` (like any function call that is not .get for examples) has no narrowing subject, so exhaustiveness analysis does not accumulate the `Ok` / `Err` negated narrows. Assigning the awaited value to a local gives Pyrefly a `NarrowingSubject::Name`, and the analysis works.

body_text:
### Describe the Bug

You can assign me to this, I will PR.

Pyrefly does not consider a nested class pattern inside a generic wrapper class exhaustive.
A common result-like pattern:
```python
match result:
    case Ok(value):
        ...
    case Err(SomeError()):
        ...
```
still leaves Pyrefly thinking the `Err[SomeError]` case can fall through.
### Repro
```python
from typing import assert_never
class Ok[T]:
    __match_args__ = ("value",)
    value: T
class Err[E]:
    __match_args__ = ("value",)
    value: E
class NotFound:
    pass
def f(r: Ok[int] | Err[NotFound]) -> int:
    match r:
        case Ok(value):
            return value
        case Err(NotFound()):
            raise Exception()
def g(r: Ok[int] | Err[NotFound]) -> int:
    match r:
        case Ok(value):
            return value
        case Err(NotFound()):
            raise Exception()
        case _:
            assert_never(r)
```
### Actual Behavior
Pyrefly reports `bad-return` for `f`:
```text
ERROR Function declared to return `int`, but one or more paths are missing an explicit `return` [bad-return]
```
For `g`, Pyrefly reports that the fallback is still reachable:
```text
ERROR Argument `Err[NotFound]` is not assignable to parameter `arg` with type `Never`
```
### Expected Behavior
Both functions should pass.
Since `r` has type:
```python
Ok[int] | Err[NotFound]
```
and the match handles:
```python
case Ok(value)
case Err(NotFound())
```
there should be no remaining possible value for the fallback.
### Keyword Pattern Variant Also Fails
The equivalent keyword pattern also fails:
```python
def h(r: Ok[int] | Err[NotFound]) -> int:
    match r:
        case Ok(value=value):
            return value
        case Err(value=NotFound()):
            raise Exception()
        case _:
            assert_never(r)
```

This seems related to match exhaustiveness, but it is not fixed by the issue #1286 fix. That fix handles direct union subjects like `A | B`; this case involves eliminating an outer generic wrapper arm based on an exhaustive nested pattern on its matched attribute.
Possibly relevant implementation details:
- Positional class patterns appear to have a TODO around narrowing attributes from `__match_args__`.
- Keyword class patterns already create an attribute/facet subject, but the narrowed facet becoming impossible does not seem to eliminate the containing wrapper type.

### Describe the Bug

This was a hard one to title.

I am trying to type my Polars DataFrame function code to support to similar kinds of dataframes, and I have a minimal working example. `DataFrame` is an in-memory object, while a `LazyFrame` is not. They cannot be joined together, but have a lot of similar methods. Two DataFrames or two LazyFrames can be joined.

It is a common pattern to write functions that are generic over these two types, always returning the same type, e.g.

```python
from typing import TypeVar
import polars as pl

Frame = TypeVar("Frame", pl.DataFrame, pl.LazyFrame)


def join_them(df1: Frame, df2: Frame) -> Frame:
    return df1.join(df2)
```
or, equivalently in the modern syntax:

```python
def join_them[Frame: (pl.DataFrame, pl.LazyFrame)](df1: Frame, df2: Frame) -> Frame:
    return df1.join(df2)
```

body_text:
We've come up with a training recipe for 2:4 activation sparsity, which is outlined in this paper: https://openreview.net/pdf?id=O5feVk7p6Y

The gist of this approach is that:

1) we find high level of activation sparsity (> 85%) when training SquaredRELU based FFNs instead of SwiGLU FFNs. These Squared-RELU based FFNs show minimal to no accuracy loss. 
2) We accelerate the sparse activation x dense weight matmul with 2:4 sparsity. We can naively sparsity for the forwards pass, dropping values to fit the 2:4 constraint if they do not fit. For the backwards pass, we need some special sauce to mantain accuraccy. 

However @janeyx99 pointed out to me that instead of accelerating the model using 2:4 sparsity, we can seek to exploit (1) with activation compression instead. The idea here is that we can use something like [nvcomp](https://developer.nvidia.com/nvcomp) to compress the sparse squared-relu activations. 

We should run some tests to know what compression ratio and thus the memory savings we could achieve, as well as if there's additional overhead for the compression to account for.
title: Accelerate activation sparsity with activation compression
